chapters.title: Chapter 1: What Momentum and Trend Following Actually Are

lessons.title: Case Study: Spotting Momentum in Nifty 50 Stocks Over a Market Cycle

children.text: The first three lessons in this chapter defined momentum in theory. Real markets don't hand you a clean, multi-decade academic sample, they hand you a cycle: a crash, a recovery, a correction, and a fresh bull run, often inside a handful of years. Nifty 50 investors between 2020 and 2024 lived through exactly this kind of cycle. This case study walks through what momentum actually looked like in each phase, including the phase where it hurt the most.

body.text: Momentum does not perform the same way in every market environment. It tends to work best in a sustained trending market, tends to suffer its sharpest losses in the violent reversal right after a market bottom, and can chop sideways or lose money through a regime change. Reading which phase of the cycle you are in matters as much as the momentum signal itself.

body.title: Nifty 50: an illustrative round-trip, 2020-2024 (approximate, rounded index levels)

children.text: Phase 1: The March 2020 Crash, a Textbook Momentum Crash

The Nifty 50 fell roughly 38% between its January 2020 peak and its March 2020 low, in about five weeks. A cross-sectional momentum portfolio built just before the crash would have been long the pre-crash winners, often quality and defensive names, and short the pre-crash laggards, often high-beta cyclicals and PSU banks. The crash itself hurt nearly everything. The real damage to the momentum strategy came after, in the sharp V-shaped recovery of April to June 2020, when the market's most beaten-down, high-beta names rebounded the fastest, considerably faster than the more defensive names that had been the strategy's long leg. A portfolio that is short the names rebounding hardest loses money on that leg exactly when the long leg is only recovering modestly, a painful combination even while the broader market is rallying.

body.label: Nifty 50, Jan-Mar 2020
body.context: One of the fastest drawdowns in the index's history, and the setup for the momentum crash that followed in the recovery

body.text: This is not a coincidence specific to 2020. Academic research on momentum crashes, notably Daniel and Moskowitz's 2016 paper 'Momentum Crashes', finds that momentum's worst losses cluster systematically around exactly this kind of moment: a sharp market rebound following a bear market bottom, when past losers rebound faster than past winners.

children.text: Phase 2: The 2020-2021 Bull Run, Momentum's Best Environment

Once the initial crash-recovery whiplash passed, the Nifty 50 entered a long, comparatively smooth uptrend from mid-2020 through October 2021, roughly doubling off its March 2020 low. This is momentum's ideal environment: a sustained trend with a clear leadership group. Indian IT services stocks, riding a global work-from-home driven demand surge, were among the clearest sustained momentum leaders of this phase, posting strong, persistent outperformance over many consecutive months rather than one sharp spike. A simple trailing-return ranking system, run monthly through this window, would have kept rotating into IT and related growth names and stayed there for most of the phase, exactly the kind of steady, low-drama outcome momentum is designed to produce.
Phase 3: The 2022 Correction, a Regime Change That Punishes Momentum

From its October 2021 peak, the Nifty 50 fell roughly 18% to its June 2022 low, as global central banks, the US Federal Reserve leading the way, hiked interest rates sharply and FIIs sold Indian equities heavily to fund that shift. This is a regime change, not a simple market decline: the richly valued growth and IT names that had led the 2020-2021 rally were hit especially hard, since higher rates disproportionately hurt stocks priced on distant future earnings, while some previously lagging value and PSU names began quietly outperforming. A momentum strategy still holding the old leadership group into this shift would have been positioned exactly wrong, a reminder that momentum tracks what has been working, not what is about to work next.

children.text: Phase 4: The 2023-2024 Bull Run, Fresh Trends Take Over

By 2023, a new leadership group had emerged, and it looked nothing like the 2020-2021 group. PSU banks and PSU stocks broadly, defence manufacturers, railway and infrastructure plays, and renewable energy names, Suzlon Energy from Lesson 1 among them, drove sustained multi-quarter rallies as the Nifty 50 pushed to new highs through September 2024. A momentum ranking system rebuilt fresh each month would have rotated into this new leadership group as it emerged, without needing to know in advance that PSU and infrastructure stocks, largely written off during the 2020-2021 growth rally, were about to become the market's strongest performers. That is the core practical advantage of momentum: it does not require forecasting which sector leads next, only recognizing that leadership has changed once the data shows it.
What This Cycle Teaches About Trading Momentum

Across all four phases, the same signal, rank securities by recent return and follow the leaders, produced very different outcomes depending purely on the market's regime. It worked cleanly through a sustained trend. It was dangerous right at a sharp turning point. It struggled through a regime change. And it adapted well once a new, sustained trend took hold. None of this means momentum is unreliable. It means momentum is regime dependent, and a trader who understands which phase of the cycle they are likely in has a real edge over one applying the same signal blindly through every market condition.

columns.label: When Momentum Works Well

A sudden regime change, like a rate-hike driven correction
A crowded trade where everyone holds the same leaders
A sharp spike in market-wide volatility

body.title: Why did the momentum portfolio struggle after March 2020?
body.question: A cross-sectional momentum portfolio was long pre-crash winners and short pre-crash losers heading into the March 2020 crash. Why did it perform poorly during the April-June 2020 recovery specifically, even though the broader market was rallying?
options: Because the market never actually recovered in this period
Because the short leg, made up of beaten-down high-beta names, rebounded faster than the long leg of more defensive winners
Because momentum strategies are not allowed to hold short positions in India
Because the Nifty 50 stopped trading during this period
body.explanation: The short leg rebounding faster than the long leg is precisely the mechanism behind a momentum crash: past losers, often high-beta and heavily beaten down, snap back hardest in a sharp market recovery, hurting a long-short momentum portfolio's short side badly.

body.title: Reading a regime change
body.scenario: It is mid-2022. You have been running a momentum strategy that has performed well for two years, consistently long IT and growth names. Over the past two months, this same strategy has started losing money steadily, even on days the Nifty 50 is flat.
body.prompt: Based on this chapter, what is the most likely explanation, and what would you want to check before concluding the strategy itself is broken?
body.modelAnswer: The most likely explanation is a regime change: rising interest rates were hitting richly valued growth and IT names disproportionately hard in 2022, while previously lagging value and PSU names were starting to outperform. The strategy losing money while the index is flat suggests its holdings, the old leadership group, are underperforming a newly emerging leadership group, not that the ranking process itself is broken. Before concluding the strategy is broken, it would be worth checking whether the strategy's holdings are still being refreshed and re-ranked on schedule, since a momentum system that adapts to new leadership should eventually rotate into the new winners rather than staying stuck in the old ones.

cards.definition: A sharp, sudden reversal in a momentum strategy's returns, typically clustering around sharp market rebounds after a bear market bottom.
A market decline followed by an unusually fast rebound, the exact environment in which momentum crashes are most likely to occur.
A structural shift in market conditions, such as a change in interest rate direction, that can flip which group of stocks is leading and which is lagging.
In a long-short momentum portfolio, the long leg holds the top-ranked past winners and the short leg holds the bottom-ranked past losers.
A shift in market leadership from one group of stocks or sectors to another, which a momentum strategy is designed to follow once the data confirms it.

points: Momentum's performance is regime dependent: strong in a sustained trend, dangerous right after a sharp market bottom, and often weak through a regime change.
The March 2020 crash and its V-shaped recovery is a textbook momentum crash: past losers rebounded faster than past winners, hurting a long-short momentum portfolio's short leg specifically.
The 2020-2021 bull run, led by IT stocks, shows momentum's ideal environment: a sustained trend with clear, stable leadership.
The 2022 correction shows momentum's weak spot: a sudden regime change can flip market leadership and punish a strategy still holding the old winners.
The 2023-2024 rally, led by PSU, defence, railway, and renewable energy names including Suzlon Energy, shows momentum adapting to a completely new leadership group once the data confirmed the shift.
This chapter's core lesson: momentum works by systematically following leadership as it changes, not by forecasting in advance which sector leads next.
